title: Checkpoint — Pause Before We Invest
tagline: A deliberate stop. You've finished the defensive game — budgeting, the emergency fund, credit and CIBIL. Let's consolidate and make sure you're ready before the heavier investment modules.
summary: A recap of Modules 1–3, a readiness checklist, and an invitation to ask questions before Module 4.

paragraphs: Stop here for a moment — this pause is intentional. You've now completed the **defensive game**: the part of personal finance that keeps money you've earned. What comes next (asset classes, goal-based investing, taxation) is the **offensive game**, and it only works if the defence is solid.

So before we touch a single mutual fund, let's make sure the foundation is in place and clear up anything fuzzy. **If any concept from Modules 1–3 is still unclear, this is the moment to revisit it or ask your questions.** The investing modules will assume you're comfortable with everything below.

blocks.title: Why we pause exactly here
blocks.text: Most people fail at investing not because they pick the wrong fund, but because they had no budget, no emergency fund, or expensive card debt quietly draining them. Fixing the foundation first is what makes the investing actually stick.

items.detail: A realistic budget (Aarav's ~75/10/15 on ₹20k), pay-yourself-first automation, and an emergency fund of ₹60,000 parked safely in a liquid fund / sweep-in FD.
Interest on interest; the Rule of 72; Time Value of Money; and the proof that starting at 22 beats starting at 30 by over ₹1.7 crore on the same monthly amount.
Credit cards as interest-free 45-day money if paid in full; the minimum-due trap; and a from-zero plan to a 750+ CIBIL score using a secured card and perfect repayment.

blocks.title: The readiness checklist before Module 4
items: I have a written monthly budget and a fixed amount auto-invested on salary day.
I have started (or am actively building) a 3–6 month emergency fund in a safe, liquid place.
I have NO high-interest debt — especially no revolving credit-card balance at ~40%.
I understand that long-term money must beat inflation, so it can't sit idle in a savings account.
I know that early, consistent investing matters more than large, late investing.

items.title: Module 4 — The Investment Arsenal
items.detail: Every asset class on the table: FDs/RDs, active vs index mutual funds, direct equity, and gold/SGBs — plus expense ratios and why Direct funds beat Regular ones.

items.title: Module 5 — Goal-Based Investing
items.detail: Matching the asset to the timeline, and a concrete step-up SIP plan for Aarav's 2031 car down payment over a strict 5-year horizon.

items.title: Module 6 — Taxation
items.detail: Old vs New regime, capital gains (LTCG vs STCG) on equity, and how tax harvesting trims your bill.

blocks.text: If the checklist above feels true, you're genuinely ready — and ahead of most people twice your age. If anything is shaky, revisit that lesson now. When you're set, continue to Module 4.

cheatsheet: Defence (budget, emergency fund, no high-interest debt) must be solid before offence (investing).
Clear any revolving credit-card debt first — no investment reliably beats ~40% card interest.
Confirm: budget automated, emergency fund building, no toxic debt, long-term money set to beat inflation.
If a Module 1–3 concept is still unclear, this is the moment to revisit it before continuing.
Next up: asset classes (M4), the 2031 car plan (M5), and taxation (M6).

questions.prompt: Aarav has ₹0 emergency fund and a ₹20,000 credit-card balance he's been paying the minimum on. He's excited to start a ₹3,000 equity SIP. What should he do first, and why?
questions.hint: Compare the card's interest rate to any realistic investment return.
answer: He should clear the credit-card balance first — it's costing ~36–45% per year, and **no realistic investment reliably returns more than that**. Paying off 40% debt is a guaranteed, tax-free 40% 'return'. Starting a 12% SIP while carrying 40% debt is mathematically losing money.

Order of operations: (1) stop adding to the card and pay it off, (2) build at least a starter emergency fund, (3) then begin the SIP. This is exactly why the course puts defence before offence — and why we paused here.
keyPoints: Clear ~40% card debt before investing at ~12%

questions.prompt: Of the five readiness-checklist items, which one is most often the real reason people's investing plans collapse, and why?
questions.hint: Think about what forces someone to sell investments at the worst time.
answer: Usually the **emergency fund** (and closely related, carrying high-interest debt). Without a buffer, the first unexpected expense forces you to either redeem investments at a bad time or swipe a credit card at ~40% — both of which can undo years of progress. A solid emergency fund is what lets your investments stay invested through life's shocks, so it's the linchpin of the whole offensive game.
keyPoints: Emergency fund is the usual failure point
No buffer → forced bad selling or expensive debt
